# Check-in 2: speaker notes

## Slide cover: Check-in 2: the method gate

Cover. One sentence: today we show how we work the data, follow one broken trade through the platform, and ask to be cleared to build the full analysis. Every number on the slides is written by a script from notebook 02's outputs (register checksum d7e752f55f0a).

## Slide 1: Our rebuild runs on all 1.41M trades, and 98.7% of the positions we can test agree across all three sources

This is the answer first. We rebuilt every holding by adding up its trades from zero: BUY adds, SELL subtracts. That ran on all 1,409,533 trade rows in 62 s, live in notebook 02.

Then we compared three sources for every position: our rebuild, the book of record (the platform's own list of holdings) and the custodian (the outside bank that holds the securities). 471,583 of the 478,026 positions we can test agree in all three: 98.7%.

We leave 2,836 positions out of that rate on purpose: we can't test them, mostly because one of their trades has a blank quantity (2,791). Unknown is not wrong and not right, so it sits beside the rate, not inside it (D-046).

5,539 positions disagree. We give each one cause; 2,605 have no cause yet and stay visible. And agreement is not proof: 637 agreeing positions contain a negative BUY. That is the trade we follow on slide 6.

Sources: 02_row_ledger.csv (load transactions), 02_run_info.csv (runtime), 02_three_way_summary.csv (all three agree; not evaluable rows), 02_break_classes.csv (is a break = yes; cause unexplained; sign_conflict_keys on all three agree).

## Slide 2: Cleaning the trades raises the differences with the book, because the book counts duplicate trade copies that we count once

How we got to our rebuild, step by step. Each bar counts positions where a rebuild differs from the book of record. Every row as delivered: 5,880 of 480,870. The Guide's shared benchmark, BOOKED rows only: 1,625 of 480,862. Our chain: 3,656 of 480,862.

Our chain is stricter than the benchmark in one main way: when the same trade arrives twice, we count it once. 2,060 trades arrived twice; both copies came in together and were published twice, a median 5 minutes apart, which looks like a resend (inferred). The book counts both copies on 2,053 of 2,053 positions that hold one. Counting both, as the book does, would add 2,032 matches, about the size of the 2,031 extra differences against the benchmark.

So more differences here is not a worse rebuild: it shows a convention of the book that we question (D-044, faculty question 4).

Sources: 02_waterfall.csv (C0, BOOKED-only, C7 vs positions: different, keys in union); 02_duplicate_profile.csv; 02_sensitivities.csv (copies: both counted).

## Slide 3: Where the data is unclear, we chose the cautious reading and measured the other one

Every choice we made, with the other reading and its effect, measured by rerunning the whole chain with that one step swapped. The effect is the change in positions that match the book, out of 480,862.

REVERSED: we keep the original and read REVERSED as a status (R1, the Guide's benchmark). Offsetting each original once (R3) changes +2 matches; offsetting every REVERSED row (R4, what the book seems to do) +681, but that is a double offset, so we never use it.

Copies: we count a trade once; counting both +2,032. Negative quantities: we keep the sign and flag it; the absolute value −638. Copies that disagree with each other are not evaluable; keeping the first changes +3.

Blank quantities: we can't test them. Counting a blank as zero adds 2,611 matches, but the money and price in the same row give the size: then 2,778 of 2,797 become testable; 0 match the book. So the book seems to drop the units of real trades (D-047). Settlement date instead of trade date: −59,970.

Sources: 02_sensitivities.csv (matched vs main chain, vs positions); 02_blank_quantity.csv (positions); 02_waterfall.csv (C7s minus C7 matched).

## Slide 4: On 3,637 positions the book and the custodian agree with each other, but not with the trades

Three sources for every position, 480,862 in all. 471,583 agree in all three. The chart shows the rest, by who disagrees.

The biggest group is the turning point of our story: on 3,637 positions the book and the custodian hold the same number, and our trades say something else. Normally two sources agreeing means we trust the number. Here the custodian seems to follow the book's own conventions, counting duplicate copies and subtracting every REVERSED row, so its agreement is not independent. Slide 5 shows which conventions.

The custodian is the odd one out on 1,886. Book against custodian alone: 480 positions are in the book only, 0 at the custodian only; for 478 of those our trades exist and agree with the book on 475, which points to a gap in the custodian's file (inferred).

Sources: 02_three_way_summary.csv (rebuild vs book vs custodian patterns; book vs custodian rows).

## Slide 5: Most breaks have a named cause; the 2,605 we can't explain stay visible

A break is a difference that must be explained; it is not automatically an error. Each of the 5,539 breaks gets exactly one cause. The rules are tested in a fixed order that we wrote in the config before counting, and the first rule that fits wins, so nothing is counted twice.

The two big named causes are conventions the book and custodian seem to share: counting duplicate copies, and subtracting every REVERSED row. Whether these are defects or intended is a question for you (slide 10), so they are unresolved, not errors.

2,605 breaks fit no rule, mostly where the custodian disagrees with both the book and the trades (1,886). We show them rather than force them into a class; opening them is our first task after today.

Flags sit on top of the class: 637 positions that agree three ways still contain a negative BUY. That's where the next slide starts.

Sources: 02_break_classes.csv (is a break = yes, keys by cause; sign_conflict_keys on all three agree).

## Slide 6: A broken trade passes every check after the point where it entered

At Check-in 1 we followed a clean trade: it passed every check (small picture, top left). Today we follow a broken one, TXN100052151, picked by a written rule, not by hand.

Observed: it is a BUY of −1,995 shares, sent by OMS_FRONT and booked. A quantity is never negative, so the record is wrong for sure. The money paid confirms the size but not the side, so two readings fit: wrong sign (a BUY of the positive amount) or wrong type (a SELL). We lean to wrong sign: of the 5 negative BUYs that have a second record, all 5 support it. But this trade has none.

The book holds −9,688 and so does the custodian, so every later check passes: the reconciliation, the custodian, the price, the NAV arithmetic. If the sign is wrong the holding should be −5,698: an exposure of about 19 basis points of the fund's net assets. If the type is wrong, zero. Exposure, never a loss. The only place to stop it is at trade capture: reject a quantity that isn't above zero.

Sources: 02_trace.csv (all hops); 02_negative_partners.csv; figures 06 and 08.

## Slide 7: The fund arithmetic fails on 40 of 2,000 rows, and 10 securities have vendor prices about 100 times apart

The brief asks for proposed checks on price data and ledger arithmetic. We ran two of them on the full data and wrote the rest as rules with a denominator.

Ledger arithmetic: for every fund share class, net assets divided by shares outstanding must equal the NAV per share, the price investors buy and sell at. It fails on 40 of 2,000 rows. Which input is wrong we can't tell yet.

Vendor prices: on the snapshot date the held securities have quotes from three vendors on 5,970 securities, from two on 30 and from none on 15. On 388 of 6,000 securities their prices differ by more than 0.5%; 15 have no quote to compare. On 10 the highest and lowest are about 100 times apart (ratio 80 to 125), the signature of a price per 100 against per unit. We flag it and never correct it automatically. Thresholds live in the config; judges can change them.

Proposed, not run: coverage (does every holding have a price), freshness (is the price from the right day and time), FX rates (the USD rate is not exactly 1: question for you).

Sources: 02_nav_check.csv (result); 02_vendor_check.csv (result); config/reconciliation.toml [prices].

## Slide 8: Five defect classes go forward, and one flag turned out to be fine

The defect catalog: five classes with a full write-up (rule, where it entered, why it matters, the fix), spread across trade capture, the pipeline, master data and the custodian feed. Each names the check that would stop it and its owner.

Negative BUYs: 655 of 1,406,714 trade rows; the record is confirmed wrong, its correct value is not. Blank quantities: the size is still in the row on 2,802 of 2,819, and the book drops the units on 2,756 of 2,778 testable positions. Duplicate copies: the book and custodian count them on 2,021 positions. Spin-off targets: 23 of 23 new securities were never set up, then traded and held without a price. Custodian gaps: 480 positions in the book have no custodian record.

The cleared flag: 42 positions whose trades net to zero and that neither source lists. Rule written before looking: a closed position isn't listed. Independent evidence: neither source stores a single zero-quantity row anywhere. What would reopen it: one zero row, or a later record.

The register behind it has 39 findings (backup B3).

Sources: 02_defect_register.csv (the six lines named in the table and bullet); 02_blank_quantity.csv; docs/DEFECT_CATALOG.md.

## Slide 9: 118 of 200 corporate actions can be applied; 82 are held back because a term we need is missing

Corporate actions are company events that change holdings: a split, a merger, a spin-off, a dividend, a redemption. For each type we wrote down the terms it needs before counting (the Guide's conventions).

118 of 200 events have every term they need. 82 are held back: mergers name no resulting security, redemptions have no rule for the units that disappear, and spin-offs point to a new security that was never set up. Held back means we don't apply them and we don't guess; the table says what would release each one.

87 of 200 events have an ex-date after their effective date. We flag them as unresolved rather than hold them back, because it depends on how the dates are defined: a question for you.

The event-adjusted holdings come in the final, kept apart from the trade-only rebuild so nothing is counted twice.

Sources: 02_ca_readiness.csv (action_type, verdict, reason codes); 02_defect_register.csv (ex_date after effective_date).

## Slide 10: We ask to be cleared to build the full analysis, and need your view on 8 questions

What we ask today: clear us to build the full analysis on this method.

The questions, by topic. Each one changes a decision. If REVERSED has a contract, or the book's conventions are intended, two of our break causes become explained instead of defects. The order side or cash direction settles every negative BUY. The date definitions decide the 87 flagged corporate actions. The rest is how we work.

What we know we haven't done yet, and will do next: open the groups we have only counted (the unexplained breaks, the positions with no trades, the rebooks that keep the old amount, the NAV fails and vendor flags); then scores with coverage, stress tests and the executive view for Check-in 3.

Questions in full: docs/STATUS.md, 'Open questions for faculty' (numbers in brackets in the table's first column map to it).

## Slide B1: The two biggest moves both copy the book: counting copies twice and counting blanks as zero

Backup. All 11 alternative readings, each swapping one step of our chain. Only two move the match with the book by more than a thousand positions: counting both copies of a trade (+2,032) and counting a blank quantity as zero (+2,611). Both copy what the book seems to do, so a better match there tells us how the book is built, not that the reading is right. Every REVERSED reading moves fewer than a thousand, so our REVERSED choice barely changes the result.

Sources: 02_sensitivities.csv (compared with positions, matched vs main chain).

## Slide B2: Reading REVERSED the other way (R3) changes the outcome of 5 of the 699 positions with a reversal

Backup. Our main reading (R1) keeps the original trade and treats REVERSED as a status. The other reading (R3) offsets each original once. We reran the 699 positions that have a REVERSED row under R3: 694 land in the same place. The rest move a little either way. So the choice matters little for the numbers; what it needs is a contract that says what REVERSED means (question 1).

Sources: 02_reversed_side_view.csv.
